triage.name: Beriberi
triage.reason: Thiamine deficiency presenting with neuropathy, high-output heart failure or edema; reachable from diet and alcohol history plus exam.

demographics: More common in populations where polished white rice is the staple food
In the US, most often seen in people with chronic alcohol use disorder
Also occurs after bariatric surgery, in prolonged parenteral nutrition without thiamine, and in severe malnutrition

risk_factors.text: Diet consisting mainly of polished white rice
Bariatric surgery or other malabsorptive gastrointestinal surgery
Prolonged parenteral nutrition without thiamine supplementation

exposures: Long-term consumption of polished white rice as the main food

chief_complaints.text: My feet feel numb and tingly
My legs feel weak and heavy
My legs and feet are swollen
I get short of breath just walking across the room

hpi.progression: Numbness and tingling start in the feet and spread upward; weakness and swelling develop later; without treatment, symptoms worsen and can involve the heart
hpi.location: Feet and legs first, then hands and arms; swelling in the lower legs and feet
hpi.radiation: Numbness spreads from the feet upward in a stocking-glove pattern
hpi.quality: Tingling, pins-and-needles, burning, and heaviness; swelling is soft and pitting
hpi.severity: Mild at first, then moderate to severe as weakness and swelling progress

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the feet and legs

pertinent_negatives: Sudden weakness on one side of the body

positives.text: Swelling of the legs and feet

negatives: Sudden weakness on one side of the body

atypical.how_it_differs: Infantile beriberi presents with vomiting, irritability, and heart failure; the classic numbness and tingling are not described.
missing_classic_features: Numbness and tingling in the feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to aging or other conditions; heart failure and confusion can be more prominent.
Hyperemesis gravidarum and poor diet can cause thiamine deficiency; presenting symptoms may be severe vomiting, weakness, and heart failure.

general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, steady gait but unsteady on tandem walking, no distress
general.severe: Ill-appearing, dyspneic on minimal exertion, needs help to stand from a chair, may be orthopneic
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, tachypneic and diaphoretic, sitting upright, confused or lethargic

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot and the medial malleolus for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower legs and feet, often symmetric and extending to the mid-calf

findings.maneuver: Test pinprick, light touch and vibration in a stocking-glove distribution, comparing distal to proximal
findings.finding: Reduced pinprick, light touch and vibration sense in a symmetric stocking-glove pattern, worse distally

findings.maneuver: Tap the Achilles tendon with the patient relaxed and the foot dorsiflexed
findings.finding: Reduced or absent ankle jerk reflexes, often symmetric

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to walk on heels and toes, and to dorsiflex the foot against resistance
findings.finding: Symmetric distal weakness, worse in the legs than the arms, with difficulty heel-walking

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking and ask them to walk heel-to-toe
findings.finding: Wide-based, unsteady gait with impaired tandem walking

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and count the rate for a full minute
findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia at rest

findings.maneuver: Measure the blood pressure and compare the systolic and diastolic values
findings.finding: Widened pulse pressure from a high-output state

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 30–45 degrees
findings.finding: Jugular venous distension above the sternal angle

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell while the patient lies in the left lateral position
findings.finding: Third heart sound (S3 gallop)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung bases posteriorly with the patient sitting upright
findings.finding: Fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases

findings.maneuver: Percuss the liver span and palpate below the right costal margin
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged liver

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place and time, and test short-term recall
findings.finding: Disorientation or impaired short-term memory, sometimes with confabulation

findings.maneuver: Test extraocular movements and observe for nystagmus
findings.finding: Horizontal nystagmus or lateral rectus weakness (Wernicke encephalopathy)
Afebrile

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the legs and feet
findings.finding: No rash, ulcers or cellulitis

findings.maneuver: Test strength and sensation on both sides and check for facial asymmetry
findings.finding: No sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop or dysarthria

labs.caveat: Mild lactic acidosis from impaired oxidative metabolism in thiamine deficiency; resolves quickly with thiamine.
Elevated in wet beriberi with high-output heart failure; a normal value argues against significant cardiac involvement.
Alternative to BNP; elevated in wet beriberi.
Low from malnutrition and chronic alcohol use; contributes to edema but is not diagnostic.
Low B12 can mimic the neuropathy of dry beriberi and often coexists in alcohol use disorder; check before attributing neuropathy to thiamine alone.
Low folate is common in malnutrition and alcohol use and can worsen neuropathy.
Hypomagnesemia is common in alcohol use disorder and must be corrected for thiamine therapy to work.
Hypophosphatemia from malnutrition; can worsen weakness and cardiac function.
Hypokalemia from poor intake, vomiting or diuretics; correct before attributing all weakness to thiamine deficiency.
Low bicarbonate from lactic acidosis or alcohol-related ketosis.
Elevated from alcohol-related liver injury, not from beriberi itself.
Supports chronic alcohol use; not specific to beriberi.
Macrocytosis from alcohol, folate or B12 deficiency rather than thiamine deficiency.
Thrombocytopenia from alcohol-related marrow suppression or liver disease.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and because hyperemesis gravidarum is a cause of thiamine deficiency.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Resting tachycardia out of proportion to fever or anemia
Low-voltage QRS complexes in the limb leads
Nonspecific T-wave flattening or inversion
Prolonged QTc interval
First-degree AV block
Atrial fibrillation

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected wet beriberi with dyspnea, edema or tachycardia

findings.text: High cardiac output with normal or increased ejection fraction
Biventricular chamber enlargement with normal wall thickness
Reduced ejection fraction in late or fulminant disease
Pulmonary venous congestion or pleural effusions

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy with confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia

findings.text: T2 hyperintensity in the medial thalami and periventricular regions
T2 hyperintensity around the third ventricle and periaqueductal gray

initial.why: Baseline blood counts; macrocytosis and thrombocytopenia point to alcohol or other vitamin deficiencies
Electrolytes, renal function and bicarbonate before thiamine and fluid therapy
Hypomagnesemia is common in alcohol use disorder and blocks the response to thiamine
Hypophosphatemia from malnutrition worsens weakness and cardiac function
Mild lactic acidosis supports thiamine deficiency and tracks severity
Rules out pregnancy and identifies hyperemesis gravidarum as a cause
Assesses chamber size, ejection fraction and cardiac output in suspected wet beriberi
initial.only_if: dyspnea, edema or tachycardia suggests cardiac involvement

confirmatory.why: Direct measure of thiamine status; low level confirms the diagnosis
Functional assay; low activity with a rise after thiamine pyrophosphate confirms deficiency

supporting.why: Low B12 causes a similar neuropathy and often coexists
Low folate is common in malnutrition and alcohol use
Reflects nutritional status and contributes to edema
Supports heart failure when the cause of dyspnea is unclear

supporting.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
supporting.only_if: confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia is present

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of neuropathy or edema
Not needed unless there is epigastric pain
Not indicated for high-output heart failure without chest pain or ischemic features

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy
not_indicated.only_if: confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia is present

decision_points: Give IV thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Correct magnesium, potassium and phosphate alongside thiamine; thiamine is ineffective when magnesium is low
Distinguish dry beriberi (neuropathy) from wet beriberi (high-output heart failure) because the workup and urgency differ
Pregnancy test before imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

differential.name: Wernicke encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Same thiamine-deficient patient population; shares ataxia and can coexist with beriberi
differential.trigger: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient

history: Acute onset over days rather than weeks to months
Heavy alcohol use or prolonged poor intake
exam: Ataxia out of proportion to sensory loss
imaging: T2 hyperintensity in medial thalami and periaqueductal gray on MRI

differential.name: Alcoholic polyneuropathy
differential.why_considered: Chronic alcohol use with symmetric distal numbness, tingling and weakness

history: Painful burning feet, often worse at night
exam: Distal weakness and absent ankle reflexes
No edema, tachycardia or signs of heart failure

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.why_considered: Symmetric paresthesias and gait difficulty with distal sensory loss

history: Vegan diet, pernicious anemia or gastric surgery
exam: Spasticity and hyperreflexia rather than absent reflexes

differential.name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Symmetric stocking-distribution numbness, tingling and burning feet

history: No heavy alcohol use or polished-rice diet
exam: Distal sensory loss with preserved strength early
labs: Elevated hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose

differential.name: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea on exertion, leg edema and tachycardia

history: Known coronary disease, hypertension or valve disease
imaging: Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction with dilated chambers

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Generalized edema and leg swelling in a malnourished patient

history: Recent infection or known glomerular disease

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, leg swelling, weakness and slowed mentation

exam: Dry skin, bradycardia and delayed relaxation of reflexes

differential.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
differential.why_considered: Ascending weakness and areflexia in a patient with recent illness
differential.trigger: Rapidly progressive ascending weakness with areflexia after a diarrheal or respiratory illness

history: No chronic alcohol use or polished-rice diet
exam: Ascending symmetric weakness with absent reflexes
labs: Elevated CSF protein with normal cell count
imaging: Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating pattern

severity.mild: Early dry beriberi: mild distal numbness and tingling in the feet, normal gait, no weakness, no edema or cardiac symptoms
severity.moderate: Established neuropathy with stocking-glove sensory loss, absent ankle reflexes, mild distal weakness, or early wet beriberi with mild leg edema and exertional dyspnea
severity.severe: Marked distal weakness with difficulty walking or rising from a chair, or wet beriberi with resting tachycardia, significant edema, elevated BNP and cardiomegaly
severity.critical: Fulminant wet beriberi with high-output heart failure, hypotension, pulmonary edema or shock; or coexisting Wernicke encephalopathy with confusion and ophthalmoplegia

red_flags.meaning: Wernicke encephalopathy; give IV thiamine immediately before glucose

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or resting tachycardia with edema
red_flags.meaning: Fulminant wet beriberi with high-output heart failure and impending shock
Cardiac decompensation; urgent echocardiogram and thiamine
Consider Guillain-Barré syndrome or severe dry beriberi; assess respiratory function
Thiamine therapy will not work until these are corrected

complications.name: High-output heart failure and pulmonary edema
clues: Dyspnea on exertion progressing to rest
Leg edema and jugular venous distension

complications.name: Korsakoff syndrome
clues: Persistent memory loss and confabulation after Wernicke encephalopathy

complications.name: Irreversible peripheral neuropathy
clues: Months of untreated numbness and weakness
Persistent sensory loss despite thiamine repletion

complications.name: Falls and fractures from gait instability

special_populations.differences: Infantile beriberi presents with vomiting, irritability, and acute heart failure; classic stocking-glove numbness is not described. Breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers are at risk.
Hyperemesis gravidarum and poor diet can cause thiamine deficiency; presenting symptoms may be severe vomiting, weakness, and heart failure. Check thiamine status and treat early.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or other conditions; heart failure and confusion can be more prominent, and polypharmacy may worsen thiamine loss.
Dialysis removes thiamine and patients on chronic dialysis are at increased risk; supplement routinely and monitor for neuropathy and heart failure.

key_questions.question: What does a typical day of eating and drinking look like for you?
key_questions.looking_for: Diet based mainly on polished white rice, or very poor intake; identifies the thiamine-deficient diet

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic heavy alcohol use, the most common cause in the US

key_questions.question: When did the numbness and tingling start, and where did it begin?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, starting in the feet and spreading upward in a stocking-glove pattern

key_questions.question: Has the numbness spread to your hands or higher up your legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Ascending symmetric sensory loss; supports a length-dependent polyneuropathy

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weakness, trouble walking, or difficulty getting out of a chair?
key_questions.looking_for: Distal weakness worse in the legs; suggests dry beriberi

key_questions.question: Are your legs or feet swollen?
key_questions.looking_for: Pitting lower-extremity edema; suggests wet beriberi

key_questions.question: Do you get short of breath with activity, or when lying flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional dyspnea or orthopnea; points to high-output heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you had palpitations or a racing heartbeat?
key_questions.looking_for: Tachycardia or palpitations from a high-output state

key_questions.question: Have you had any confusion, trouble with memory, or double vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; suggests coexisting Wernicke encephalopathy and the need for immediate IV thiamine

key_questions.question: Have you had weight loss, poor appetite, or trouble keeping food down?
key_questions.looking_for: Malnutrition, anorexia or prolonged vomiting that predisposes to thiamine deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had any stomach or weight-loss surgery, or been on long-term IV nutrition?
key_questions.looking_for: Bariatric surgery, malabsorptive GI surgery, or parenteral nutrition without thiamine

key_questions.question: Do you take diuretics or any other regular medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Furosemide or other diuretics that increase thiamine loss and can worsen edema

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy with hyperemesis gravidarum as a cause; also needed before imaging

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of neuropathy or heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative inherited causes of neuropathy or cardiomyopathy

reasoning_points: Recognizes a diet of polished white rice or chronic heavy alcohol use as the key risk factor for thiamine deficiency
Describes the gradual, symmetric, length-dependent stocking-glove sensory loss starting in the feet
Distinguishes dry beriberi (peripheral neuropathy with distal weakness and absent ankle reflexes) from wet beriberi (high-output heart failure with edema, tachycardia and elevated BNP)
Notes that thiamine deficiency can coexist with Wernicke encephalopathy, signaled by confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus
Plans to give IV thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient
Checks and corrects magnesium, potassium and phosphate, because thiamine is ineffective when magnesium is low
Orders whole-blood thiamine diphosphate or erythrocyte transketolase activity to confirm the diagnosis
Considers and excludes look-alikes such as alcoholic polyneuropathy, vitamin B12 deficiency, diabetic neuropathy, Guillain-Barré syndrome and heart failure from other causes

easy: Classic stocking-glove numbness and tingling in a patient with a polished-rice diet or heavy alcohol use
Obvious pitting leg edema with tachycardia and exertional dyspnea
Absent ankle reflexes and distal sensory loss on exam
Low whole-blood thiamine level confirms the diagnosis
medium: Predominantly cardiac presentation with edema and dyspnea but little or no neuropathy
Neuropathy attributed to alcohol alone, missing coexisting thiamine deficiency
Coexisting B12 deficiency or hypomagnesemia that muddies the picture
Mild early symptoms with normal gait and no edema
hard: Infant with vomiting, irritability and acute heart failure rather than classic numbness
Older adult whose weakness and swelling are attributed to aging or heart failure
Pregnant patient with hyperemesis gravidarum and severe weakness
Patient on chronic dialysis or long-term parenteral nutrition without thiamine supplementation
Coexisting Wernicke encephalopathy with confusion and ophthalmoplegia dominating the presentation
